problem: Massively parallel simulators such as Isaac Lab, MJX, ManiSkill3 and Genesis cannot train vision-based RL at scale. Their photorealistic rendering either costs too much or runs out of memory, and their rasterized images are far from reality. Earlier 3DGS robotics systems (RoboGSim, GSWorld, DISCOVERSE) are single-environment evaluators rather than batched training engines. GaussGym batches 3DGS but has no dynamic 3DGS scenes and targets locomotion rather than contact-rich manipulation. Building sim-ready photorealistic assets is still mostly manual.
motivation: Tasks with rich dynamics and contacts, such as legged locomotion and contact-rich manipulation, need large-scale parallel RL. Moving these tasks to vision-centric policies requires batched photorealistic rendering that fits in GPU memory alongside training. The authors observe that pruned 3D Gaussian Splatting bound to rigid bodies can deliver near-photographic images at rasterization-like throughput. Paired with a stable large-timestep physics engine and a single-image Real2Sim pipeline, this could close both the visual and the physical sim-to-real gap.
key_idea: Couple a new velocity-impulse parallel physics engine (MotrixSim) with a pruned, batched 3DGS renderer, whose Gaussians are bound to physics rigid bodies through Rigid-Link Gaussian Kinematics, plus a single-image Real2Sim asset pipeline, so that vision-based RL runs at about 10^4 FPS over 2048 photorealistic environments on one GPU.
insight: Photorealism rather than visual randomization is what closed the visual sim-to-real gap in the one real-world test. The authors trained the same RGB PickCube PPO policy with the same network, hyperparameters and image-level randomization in four simulators. It transferred at 18/20 from GS-Playground and 0/20 from each of MuJoCo Playground, ManiSkill3 and Isaac Lab. Aggressive pruning is almost free: keeping 30% of Gaussians drops PSNR only from 27.15 to 26.87, gives 648 vs 125 FPS for a single environment, and has a negligible effect on imitation-policy success in the appendix. The physics results (shaking test 90/90 vs 60/90 for IsaacSim/Genesis; Go1 locomotion at decimation 1 matching Isaac Lab at decimation 4) indicate that strict complementarity with PGS allows larger timesteps and so higher wall-clock throughput.
method: MotrixSim physics engine: velocity-impulse formulation in generalized coordinates with soft constraints linearized into a compliance form. Equality constraints are eliminated by Schur complement, and contact/Coulomb friction is solved as an MCP with Projected Gauss-Seidel using strict complementarity and velocity clamping at friction limits. CPU and GPU backends, cross-platform, MJCF-compatible.

Solver engineering: constraint islands (disjoint interacting-body sets solved in parallel on CPU threads), and warm-starting PGS from the previous frame's impulses via contact-manifold tracking, which cuts iterations from over 50 to under 10 on stacking.

Batch 3DGS renderer: built on gsplat with simulation-oriented optimizations. Pruning inspired by PUP/Mini-Splatting/Speedy-Splat keeps about 30% of Gaussians for static scenes and removes up to 90% for dynamic objects and robot links. Reaches about 10^4 aggregate FPS for 2048 envs at 640×480.

Rigid-Link Gaussian Kinematics (RLGK): each Gaussian is assigned to a rigid body with a stored local pose. At each step a batched gather maps the B×N_bodies×7 physics poses to world poses for B×M Gaussians, broadcasting one template scene across all environments.

Real2Sim pipeline from a single RGB image: Grounding DINO + SAM/SAM2 segmentation with visual de-duplication, then iterative object removal with LaMa inpainting. Objects go through SAM-3D (3DGS + mesh + pose/scale), background through AnySplat (3DGS + depth + cameras), followed by depth/mask-area alignment and Speedy-Splat pruning. Mass and friction come from task config or domain randomization. The pipeline produced the Bridge-GS dataset from Bridge-v2.
Sensor suite: batched ray-cast LiDAR (rotating, solid-state, non-repetitive; dynamic objects; self-occlusion), height scan, RGB/depth, and MuJoCo-equivalent contact force and torque data.

Navigation demo: hierarchical PPO on Unitree Go2. A high-level policy (frozen pre-trained ViT features of a 224×224 egocentric RGB image + one-hot color command + proprioception, fed to an LSTM) outputs (vx, vy, ωyaw) at 5 Hz. A frozen pre-trained low-level locomotion policy runs at 50 Hz. Training uses a PGSR-reconstructed indoor scene with 1024 environments for 200 PPO iterations.

setting.backbone: Navigation demo: frozen pre-trained ViT encoder + LSTM actor (high-level PPO policy), with a frozen PPO-trained MLP (256-128-64) low-level locomotion controller. Manipulation: MuJoCo Playground vision-PPO CNN (encoder output 16). The paper's main contribution is a simulator, not a policy.
setting.training_data: On-policy RL inside GS-Playground: 1024 parallel envs × 200 PPO iterations for navigation in one PGSR-reconstructed indoor scene; 2048 envs for PickCube (Real2Sim-reconstructed scene); 1024/2048 envs for Go2/G1 locomotion. Domain randomization is used throughout. Also releases the Bridge-GS dataset, thousands of scenes reconstructed from Bridge-v2.
setting.observation: Navigation: egocentric monocular RGB (224×224 into ViT) + proprioception (33-d) + one-hot target color. Manipulation: two RGB cameras + joint states + target position. Platform additionally provides depth, LiDAR, height scan and contact sensing.
setting.action_space: Navigation: continuous velocity commands (vx, vy, ωyaw) at 5 Hz to a frozen 50 Hz locomotion controller. Manipulation: 6-DoF joint positions + gripper.
setting.privileged: none at test time; the asymmetric critic receives privileged states (contact forces, linear velocity, uncorrupted signals) during training only

numbers_note: No quantitative navigation metrics are reported. The Go2 red-cone visual navigation task (success when within 0.35 m of the cone, 25 s limit) is shown only qualitatively in real-world deployment and through a reward-curve figure. There are no standard embodied-navigation benchmarks (R2R, ObjectNav, etc.). Other quantitative results are system-level: about 10^4 aggregate FPS (2048 envs, 640×480, RTX 4090); single-env pruned 3DGS at 648 vs 125 FPS; 3DGS pruning table (30% Gaussians, PSNR 26.8658 / SSIM 0.8022 / LPIPS 0.2840 vs 27.1503 / 0.8296 / 0.2238); 1,015 FPS with 50 humanoids, 32× over MuJoCo and ~600× over MjWarp (1.71 FPS); hold-stage force error 0.039 mN; sim-real success correlation 0.89 for ACT/DP/π0. Rendering-throughput comparisons against Isaac Sim, Go1 locomotion wall-clock curves and multi-body stability are given only in figures.
results: GS-Playground reaches about 10^4 aggregate FPS over 2048 photorealistic 3DGS environments at 640×480 on one GPU. It beats Isaac Sim ray tracing across resolutions and GPUs, and Isaac Sim hits OOM at 1280×720. An RGB PickCube PPO policy trained in it transfers zero-shot to a real AIRBOT arm at 90% (18/20), while identically trained policies from MuJoCo Playground, ManiSkill3 and Isaac Lab all score 0/20. The physics engine keeps 90/90 grasps in the shaking test (IsaacSim/Genesis 60/90, MuJoCo ≤4/90), and runs 32× faster than MuJoCo in dense 50-humanoid scenes. Policies transfer to Go2 and G1 locomotion and to Go2 RGB cone-following navigation, but navigation is demonstrated only qualitatively.
limitations: 3DGS bakes in static lighting, so dynamic lighting is not simulated (only approximated with color jitter). Transparent and specular objects remain hard to reconstruct.
RLGK assumes rigid bodies; deformables, cloth and fluids are not supported. Physical parameters are hand-set or randomized, not estimated from images.

Navigation evaluation is a simplified single-scene red-cone goal-seeking task with no quantitative success/SPL metrics and no comparison on standard navigation benchmarks. The GPU physics backend is still less robust than the CPU backend (74/90 at dt=0.01).
